Pregnancy

How long does an epidural last during labour?

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

An epidural can provide pain relief through a long labour because medicine can be given repeatedly through a thin tube. It is usually not a single injection with one fixed expiry time. Once treatment stops, feeling and strength return gradually. The exact timing depends on the medicines, dose and your response, so your maternity team checks how well it is working and how you recover.

How long can pain relief be continued?

During labour, the catheter can stay in place so medicine can be delivered by a pump or additional doses. This allows relief to continue for hours, with adjustments as labour changes. In some circumstances it can also help with a procedure after birth. Keeping the catheter available is different from guaranteeing that one dose lasts until the baby is born.

Ask how your unit provides top-ups and how to request help if discomfort returns. Some systems have a patient-controlled button with programmed limits; others are managed by staff. Use the method you are taught and tell the team if it is not helping. A catheter can occasionally need repositioning or replacement.

An epidural is a technique, not the name of one drug

The epidural space lies outside the membrane surrounding the spinal fluid and nerves. A trained anesthesia professional places the catheter there, usually in the lower back for labour. It is not intended to enter the spinal cord. The medicine acts near nerves carrying pain signals from the lower body.

Labour solutions commonly combine a local anesthetic, which reduces nerve sensation, with a small amount of an opioid pain medicine. The balance and strength can be adjusted for the purpose. Epidural techniques are also used for some operations and postoperative pain. An epidural steroid injection for a back or leg problem is a different treatment with different expectations; its duration should not be used to predict labour pain relief.

Epidural, spinal and combined techniques differ

A spinal anesthetic usually involves a single injection into the fluid-containing space deeper than the epidural space. It works quickly and is often used for a cesarean. A labour epidural usually has a catheter through which treatment can continue.

A combined spinal–epidural uses elements of both, with rapid initial relief and an epidural catheter for later doses. These terms are not interchangeable. If you hear several names, ask which technique is proposed and what it means for onset, movement and later pain control.

When can you ask for one?

Discuss your preferences during pregnancy and tell your midwife when you want more pain relief in labour. You do not have to commit to an epidural in advance, and you can reconsider a previous plan. Whether and when it can be placed depends on your condition, the progress of labour and the service available.

Very late in labour, the baby may be born before there is time to place an epidural and obtain useful relief. Full dilation is not an automatic rule that it can never be used. In an urgent cesarean, the team considers how quickly anesthesia is needed and whether an existing block works. Sometimes another technique, including general anesthesia, is necessary.

What the team checks beforehand

Tell the anesthesia team about medicines, especially blood thinners, bleeding or clotting problems, fever, an infection near the lower back and any major illness. Give the name and timing of anticoagulant doses accurately; do not stop a prescribed medicine yourself to make an epidural possible. These details can change the timing or suitability of the procedure.

Also mention previous spine surgery, implants, a spinal condition or existing weakness and numbness. Some back problems make placement more complex, while others do not prevent it. An antenatal anesthetic appointment can help when a concern is already known, giving time to review records and discuss alternatives.

Positioning, cleaning and local numbing

You are usually awake. Staff help you sit leaning forward or lie on your side with your back curved comfortably. A drip is commonly placed so fluids or medicines can be given if needed. The anesthesia professional cleans the back with antiseptic and uses a small local-anesthetic injection to numb the skin.

That first injection may sting briefly. Afterward, you may feel pressure or discomfort while the epidural is positioned. Tell the clinician about sharp pain or an unusual shooting sensation, and let them know when a contraction is starting. Staff can help you keep a safe position; you are not expected to manage the procedure without communication or support.

The catheter stays; the placement needle comes out

A needle guides the fine catheter into the epidural space. Once the tube is positioned, the needle is removed and the catheter is secured with a dressing. Medicines are then given through the tube, with doses and checks chosen for the situation. A needle is not left in your back throughout labour.

Placing the epidural takes time, and the medicine then needs time to spread and work. Full relief often develops over about twenty to thirty minutes after dosing, although the total wait can be longer if placement is difficult or the anesthesia professional is attending another emergency. Ask what relief is available while you wait.

What you may feel while it works

The aim during labour is strong pain relief, not necessarily the disappearance of every sensation below the waist. You may still feel touch, pressure or some tightening with contractions. Your legs can feel warm, heavy, numb or less strong. The effect varies with the medicine and dose.

Low-dose approaches may allow more movement, but do not assume that a mobile epidural means you can stand or walk independently. Staff assess strength, balance and the monitoring arrangements. You can usually move your upper body and remain involved in the birth. If the urge to push feels different, the maternity team can guide you.

How the team checks and adjusts relief

Staff monitor your blood pressure and the baby’s heart rate and check the level of the block. You may be asked about cold sensation on the abdomen or legs. These checks help show whether the medicine is reaching the intended area and whether you need an adjustment.

Tell the midwife or anesthetist if contractions are still painful, the relief is only on one side or a painful patch remains. More medicine, a position change or a catheter adjustment may help; sometimes a new epidural or another option is needed. Do not assume persistent pain must be accepted because you have already received the procedure.

If an assisted birth, repair or cesarean is needed

An effective epidural can sometimes be strengthened for an assisted vaginal birth or repair of a tear. It can also sometimes be topped up with a stronger solution for a cesarean, allowing you to stay awake. The team checks the block before beginning and continues to listen to what you feel.

Pressure or movement during surgery differs from pain. Report pain promptly rather than expecting that repair or surgery is guaranteed to be painless because the catheter is present. If the epidural does not provide adequate surgical anesthesia, a spinal or general anesthetic may be needed according to urgency and the clinical assessment.

What happens after the medicine stops?

Numbness and heaviness can remain for a few hours after the final medicine is given. Tingling may occur as sensation returns. Recovery is gradual and differs between people, so staff check leg movement and feeling instead of deciding that you are ready to walk solely because a certain time has passed.

Stay sitting or lying safely until staff say it is appropriate to get up, and use the help they recommend. The bladder may need temporary drainage because you cannot clearly feel it filling. Ask about further pain relief as the block wears off. A return of discomfort can be managed; new or increasing neurological symptoms need assessment.

Side effects vary in importance

A fall in blood pressure can cause nausea or lightheadedness and may be treated with fluids or medicine. Itching, shivering, sickness or a raised temperature can occur. Tell staff about these symptoms, because fever and feeling unwell should be assessed rather than automatically attributed to the epidural.

The insertion area may feel sore for a time. A severe headache can follow an accidental puncture of the membrane around the spinal fluid and may need specific treatment. Rare complications include infection, bleeding around the spine or nerve injury. Most people do not experience serious complications, but it is inaccurate to say that all adverse effects simply disappear without treatment.

Warning signs during recovery or after discharge

Seek urgent medical assessment for new, persistent or increasing leg weakness or numbness, difficulty bearing weight, new loss of bladder or bowel control, or trouble passing urine after expected recovery. Severe or worsening back pain, fever, neck stiffness, or redness, swelling or pus at the insertion site also needs prompt help.

Report a severe or persistent headache, especially one that worsens upright and improves lying down. Not every postpartum headache comes from the epidural, so the cause needs assessment. If symptoms arise at home, contact the maternity or anesthesia service or attend an emergency department, explaining that you recently had an epidural or spinal. Do not wait for a routine follow-up when warning symptoms are present.

Plan support for comfort and baby care

Pain relief can make it easier to rest during a long labour and spend time with the baby afterward. Ask for help with positioning, skin-to-skin contact and feeds while your legs are weak or you feel unsteady. If you become sleepy while holding the baby, ask someone to transfer them to their safe sleep space.

Before discharge, ask whom to contact, what recovery should look like and how to manage ongoing pain. Include your preferences and questions in the birth plan while leaving room for changes. Choosing an epidural, needing it unexpectedly or choosing another method is not a measure of how well you cope with birth.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS and obstetric-anesthesia guidance describe catheter dosing, variable onset and gradual recovery.

Individual assessment matters for clotting concerns, medicines and previous back surgery.

NHS aftercare guidance distinguishes routine recovery from warning symptoms needing urgent assessment.

How BeMama can help

The full source’s duration, procedure, medicines, timing, eligibility, sensations, benefits and complications are retained, with corrected technique names and no guarantee of complete or indefinite relief.

When to seek help

Educational information. Obstetric-anesthetist review remains pending before publication. Follow the treating team’s monitoring, mobility and discharge instructions.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • An epidural catheter allows ongoing doses rather than one fixed-duration injection.
  • Placement and medicine onset each take time; incomplete relief should be reported.
  • Labour epidural, spinal and combined techniques are different.
  • Strength and sensation return gradually, with assisted movement until assessed.
  • Severe headache, worsening back pain or neurological changes need prompt medical review.

Frequently asked questions

Will an epidural run out before a long labour ends?

Medicine can usually be continued or topped up through the catheter. Tell the team if relief fades, because the dose or catheter may need adjustment.

How soon should it start working?

Full relief often takes about twenty to thirty minutes after medication is given, in addition to setup time. The actual timing varies.

Is the needle left in my back?

No. The placement needle is removed. A thin flexible catheter remains to deliver medicine.

Will I have no feeling at all below the waist?

Not necessarily. Pressure and touch may remain during labour, and movement varies with the dose. Tell the team about pain rather than assuming all sensation is expected.

Can I still push?

Usually you can participate in pushing, though the sensation or urge may change. Your maternity team helps with timing and positioning.

Does back surgery rule out an epidural?

Not automatically. The type of operation, any implants and current nerve symptoms need assessment, ideally during pregnancy when possible.

Can the epidural be used for a cesarean?

Sometimes a working epidural can be strengthened for surgery. If it is unsuitable or time is critical, the anesthetist may recommend another technique.

When can I walk afterward?

When staff have checked that feeling, strength and balance are adequate and agreed what assistance you need. Do not stand alone while your legs remain weak.

Should I wait for a severe headache to disappear?

No. Contact the maternity or anesthesia team for assessment, especially if it changes with posture or comes with fever, neck stiffness or other symptoms.

What if numbness or weakness returns after I go home?

Seek urgent medical assessment. New or worsening leg symptoms or bladder/bowel problems should not be treated as routine wearing-off effects.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
